chunks: Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Mismāʿ Kirdīn, said:
I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who broke the bone of a dead person. He said: “His sanctity when dead is greater than his sanctity while he is alive.”

Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan said: These reports do not contradict the first report stating that the diyah of the dead person is one hundred dinars, because there is nothing in any of these reports stating that the sanctity of the dead person is exactly like the sanctity of the living person, or that breaking his hand is more severe than breaking the hand of the living person, and whatever is of that kind in requiring diyah equal to the diyah of the living. If that is not present in them, then it is possible that what is intended is that his sanctity is like the sanctity of the living in that whoever breaks one of his limbs or cuts it deserves punishment and some portion of the diyah, even if it is not complete. This is not found with any of the dead besides the human being, so from this aspect his sanctity is like the sanctity of the living.

key_terms.الْإِنْسَانِ: the human being, singled out for this ruling
key_terms.حُرْمَتُهُ: his inviolability or sanctity in legal and moral terms
key_terms.دِيَةَ: financial compensation due for bodily injury
key_terms.عَظْمَ: bone, indicating bodily violation of the corpse
key_terms.مَيِّتًا: in the state of being deceased

ai.seo_question: What does this hadith say about breaking the bone of a dead person and the sanctity of the deceased in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith states that the sanctity of a deceased human being remains grave and inviolable, such that violating the corpse carries legal and moral consequence. The appended explanation clarifies that this does not necessarily mean the diyah is identical to that of a living person, but that the deceased human retains a special inviolability unlike other dead creatures.
